Kamal Sir handed back the fractions test. Pradeep looked at the red seven at the top and threw his pencil down. "He always gives low marks to me. He was in a bad mood today." He did not open his notebook that evening, and he said luck decides tests anyway.
Two rows away, Dilnaz had a six on the same test. She frowned at the paper, then flipped to the questions she had missed. "I didn't practise the last part." At home she did ten sums every day for a week, checking each one. The next test brought her an eight, and she grinned. Then it rained during football practice, the match was cancelled, and Dilnaz muttered, "I should have reminded everyone to come earlier." Kamal Sir overheard. "The rain isn't your job, Dilnaz. Practice and effort help a lot, but not everything is up to us." She let out a breath and put her boots in the bag. Pradeep stayed on the bench, arms folded, waiting for the next test to be unfair as well.

qa.q: How many sums did Dilnaz do every day for a week?
qa.a: She did ten sums every day for a week.

qa.q: How do Pradeep and Dilnaz explain their marks differently, and what does each do next?
qa.a: Pradeep blamed Kamal Sir's bad mood and luck, so he stopped opening his notebook. Dilnaz linked her six to not practising the last part, so she practised every day and improved to an eight.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she muttered that she should have reminded everyone to come earlier?
qa.a: She felt guilty and responsible, blaming herself for something the rain had caused.

qa.q: What could Kamal Sir say to Pradeep to help him see his part in the result?
qa.a: He could show Pradeep the questions he missed and how a little practice on them could change the next mark, without blaming him.

grounding: Two children in one class explain a test result differently: outside forces (4081) versus effort that can be changed but sometimes over-blames the self (4442).

passage:
In Lavanya Ma'am's class, reading time meant one child at a time standing up. Uday stumbled on "pyramid" and felt heat rush to his face. He crossed his eyes, wobbled his head and read the next line like a robot. The class roared, and Uday bowed. Then it was Ritu's turn. She said "hippopotamus" as "hippo-pot-a-mouse", and someone snorted. Within seconds, the whole row was repeating it in squeaky voices. Ritu smiled and even said it again herself, but she kept her eyes on her shoes, and her hands gripped the book so hard that the pages creased.
At the bell, Lavanya Ma'am asked Ritu to stay. Ritu looked at the floor. "That was a hard word, and it was unkind of the class to keep repeating it," said Lavanya Ma'am. "Was it fun for you?" Ritu shrugged, then her eyes filled. "Not really." Lavanya Ma'am nodded. "Thank you for telling me. I'll talk to the class tomorrow, and you can decide whether to be there." Ritu wiped her cheek with her sleeve and gave a small nod.

qa.q: How did Ritu say "hippopotamus" in class?
qa.a: She said it as "hippo-pot-a-mouse".

qa.q: How is Uday's laughter from the class different from the laughter Ritu got?
qa.a: Uday made the class laugh with him, and the joke kept control of his embarrassment. Ritu's mistake became the joke and the class laughed at her, so she smiled outside but shrank inside, keeping her eyes on her shoes.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she smiled and repeated the word herself?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed. Laughing along was a way to get through it, not a sign she found it funny.

qa.q: What did Lavanya Ma'am do well after class, and what could she do next?
qa.a: She stayed with Ritu, named the class's unkindness and asked how it felt. She could talk to the class the next day and check in with Ritu again.

grounding: One classroom shows a child laughing with the class as a cover (3891) and a child whose mistake made her the joke, smiling while hurting (5281).

passage:
At nine, Sabina misspelled "because" as "becuase" on a test. She stared at the red mark and cried. "The whole test is a disaster. I'm stupid." Papa Yash pointed at the eighteen out of twenty at the top, but Sabina wiped her eyes and insisted that one mistake had ruined it.
At fifteen, she looked at her hours on the phone one Sunday and felt sick. She announced to her friend Chinmay, "From tomorrow, no screens at all for a month. Not one." Chinmay raised an eyebrow. "But the class group is on messaging. The maths homework gets posted there." Sabina waved a hand. "I'll manage." On Wednesday she missed the notice about a changed test date, and her friends were confused when she did not reply. On Thursday night she opened the chat to check the homework and saw twenty-three unread messages. She sat looking at the screen. "It's finished," she said. "I broke it on the first week. I may as well scroll all night." She scrolled until late, then put the phone down without any plan for the next day.

qa.q: How many messages were unread when Sabina opened the chat on Thursday night?
qa.a: There were twenty-three unread messages.

qa.q: What thinking links Sabina's reaction to one wrong word and to opening the chat on Thursday?
qa.a: In both, one slip turns into total failure. One misspelled word made the whole test a disaster, and one peek at the chat meant the whole month was broken, so she scrolled all night.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she said "It's finished" and looked at the screen?
qa.a: She felt defeated and disappointed in herself, as if one small lapse proved she could not do it.

qa.q: What could Sabina do differently if she tries to cut back on screens again?
qa.a: She could choose a smaller change, such as a set time each day, keep the class group for homework, and count one slip as a bump, not the end.

grounding: All-or-nothing thinking over one wrong word at nine (3927) and a cold-turkey screen ban abandoned after one slip at fifteen (6526): one girl over years.

passage:
At sixteen, Disha had a geography project due on Friday, and it lay untouched. She told herself she would start when she felt inspired. Deep down she feared that a poor result would show everyone she was ordinary. So she reorganised her books, then watched a series, then went to bed. On Thursday night she scribbled something together, and the result was thin.
At twenty, the pattern was the same in her college assignment. After she handed it in late, Disha sat on her bed with her roommate Ira nearby. "I'm so lazy," she said. "Next time I'll start the day it's given. I mean it." Ira glanced up from her laptop. "You said that last month." Disha felt her face burn. The next project came, and the harsh voice in her head grew louder, which made starting feel even heavier. She opened the file twice and closed it both times. Her friend Hansa messaged, "Want to work in the library together tomorrow?" Disha looked at the message for a long moment before answering yes.

qa.q: Which day was Disha's geography project due?
qa.a: It was due on Friday.

qa.q: How does Disha's calling herself lazy at twenty connect to her delay at sixteen?
qa.a: At sixteen she put off work from fear of a poor result. At twenty she blamed herself as lazy and vowed to change, but the harsh voice made starting feel heavier, so the delay came back.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when her face burned after Ira's remark?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and defensive, because Ira's words pointed at a promise she had already broken.

qa.q: How might working with Hansa in the library help Disha?
qa.a: Sitting beside a friend can lower the dread of starting, so she can begin with a messy first part and build momentum.

grounding: An avoidant delay at sixteen (4056) becomes a loop of self-blame and vows at twenty that adds to the dread (3191): one person over years.

passage:
At nine, Yamini stood at the edge of the pool for her first swimming class. Her stomach flipped. "This pool is dangerous. I can feel it," she told Anjali Ma'am, who taught the beginners. The coach nodded gently. "That's a big feeling. Let's put our feet in first." Yamini stayed on the side for the whole session, sure that the fear itself proved the water was unsafe.
At fifteen, Yamini sat in a critical-thinking class where Anjali Ma'am, now her teacher, wrote emotional reasoning on the board. "We treat a strong feeling as proof," she explained. "I feel worried, so something must be wrong." Yamini's friend Gurleen whispered, "That's you before every test." Yamini thought of the pool. Then she thought about the coming exam and the tight feeling in her chest that told her she was sure to fail. She wrote in her notebook, "Feeling sure is not the same as knowing. Check the facts. What marks have I got in mock tests?" She looked up, half smiling. "I have been doing that my whole life," she whispered, and Gurleen giggled.

qa.q: What did Yamini say about the pool at nine?
qa.a: She said, "This pool is dangerous. I can feel it."

qa.q: How is Yamini's belief about the pool related to what she notices in the critical-thinking class?
qa.a: At nine, her strong feeling of fear made her sure the pool was dangerous, which is emotional reasoning, treating a feeling as proof. At fifteen she learns the name for it and applies it to the exam, reminding herself to check the facts.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling on the edge of the pool at her first class?
qa.a: She was scared and anxious. Her stomach flipped, and the strength of the fear convinced her the water was unsafe.

qa.q: What could Yamini do when she feels sure she will fail the exam?
qa.a: She can look at her mock-test marks and other facts, ask someone she trusts, and treat the feeling as a signal to check, not as proof.

grounding: A child treats fear of the pool as proof of danger (3944), and years later the same girl learns to spot such emotional reasoning and check the facts (80).

passage:
Ten minutes into a Sunday morning, five-year-old Uma dropped her crayons. "I'm bored. What do I do?" Mummy Deepika, who was mid-sentence on a phone call, held out the tablet without looking up. Uma took it and went quiet for an hour.
At eight, the same habit had settled. Every time Uma sighed and said she was bored, the tablet appeared within seconds. One afternoon, Papa Shankar watched it happen from the doorway and said softly, "Let's try something. Next time, we wait a little." A week later, Uma flopped on the sofa. "I'm bored." Mummy took a breath and only said, "Hmm." Five minutes passed. Uma kicked her heels, stared at the ceiling, and dragged over a basket of odd socks. She slipped a sock over her hand, then another, and started a puppet play about two socks who did not like each other. Papa Shankar clapped from the corner. Mummy Deepika laughed. The tablet stayed on the shelf, and nobody had told Uma what to do.

qa.q: What did Uma dig out of the basket to make her puppet play?
qa.a: She dragged over a basket of odd socks and slipped socks over her hand.

qa.q: How do the tablet at five and the waiting at eight show different ways an adult can respond to boredom?
qa.a: At five and again at eight, Mummy Deepika instantly gave the tablet, so the boredom was covered from outside. When she waited a few minutes and only said "Hmm", Uma's own idea, a sock puppet play, appeared.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she flopped on the sofa and said she was bored?
qa.a: She felt restless and uncomfortable, not sure yet what to do with herself.

qa.q: What could Mummy Deepika and Papa Shankar do to keep this going?
qa.a: They can keep a short wait before helping, leave simple things like socks and paper within reach, and enjoy Uma's ideas when they come.

grounding: A child's early boredom (4068) and a parent who instantly rescues with a tablet (5210), until a short unrescued wait brings out creativity.
